nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Gulf Menhaden
Scientific Name: Brevoortia patronus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthyes
      Order: Clupeiformes
      Family: Cupeidae


Other Common Names: pogy (327 1419); sardine (1419); large-scale Gulf menhaden (891) ;
Large scale menhaden ( 693 ) ; shad

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Gulf menhaden support the largest single commercial fishery (by weight) in the United States (107 638 639). Landings for 1988 were near 1.4 billion pounds valued at $73.3 million. Statewide Florida menhaden landings for 1991 were 7,027,158 lbs valued at $941,639 (902), although most of these are B. tyrannus, and B. smithi landings are probably also included in this sum. Menhaden are harvested from early April to early October as they move into more shallow inshore areas from their wintering grounds on the middle part of the continental shelf (409). Fishing grounds occur in the area extending from Apalachee, Florida to Matagorda Bay, Texas, but are concentrated in Louisiana and Mississippi waters (118 507 1464).

Schools are located by spotter planes who notify large, refrigerated carrier vessels. Two purse seine boats encircle the school with a net. The captured school is then pumped into the hold of the carrier vessel for processing (508 652). Also caught with gill nets and trawls (791). Although not highly esteemed because they are bony and very oily, they are marketed fresh, salted and canned (791). Menhaden are used primarily for the production of meal, oil, and solubles (791). Small quantities are used for bait and canned pet food .

Recreational: Has no sport fish value since it is a filter feeder with unpalatable meat (652).

Indicator: Larvae used by National Marine Fisheries Service to study uptake and effects of heavy metals on the early life stages of fishes (274).

Ecological Role: Extremely important forage fish for a variety of piscivorous birds and fish (119). piscine predators include ~ynoscion nebulosus (220). Important in the translocation of energy between estuarine and offshore ecosystems (172).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Restricted to Gulf of Mexico occurring in estuarine and nearshore marine waters to depths of 111 m from Tampa Bay, Florida to Vera Cruz, Mexico (327 788 791 823 891 983). Principal region of abundance is from Appalachicola, Florida to Galveston, Texas (119 188 327 409 565 585).

Within Study Area: Found only on the west coast of Florida from about Florida Bay north (409 565 585 788 791 891). Dahlberg (823) found B. smithi to be much more common than B. patronus in Florida west coast estuaries. Juveniles commonly occur in all estuaries from Tampa Bay northward, but decrease in numbers to the south (824 1052 1053) .

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs and larvae spend 3-5 wk in offshore waters as currents carry them into estuaries (707 791). Juveniles are nektonic and schooling. Adults are pelagic and schooling, usually found in shallow waters (172 707 751 791). Caught in waters as deep as 60 m (791). Adult migrate offshore for spawning (791 1419).

Larvae are carried from the central breeding grounds for 3-5 weeks by currents and are thought to be distributed along near shore areas throughout the range predominantly by long shore current (639). Larvae migrate into estuaries in late fall and early winter through late May with peak movement into Texas and Louisiana tidal passes occurring between November and early April. They are then carried through open bays and into shallow estuarine areas (tidal creeks and ponds) by tidal flow when ca. 15-25 nun. They may then move past the brackish-freshwater areas and utilize such areas as nursery grounds (655). As larvae metamorphose into juveniles they move into deeper, higher salinity areas of the estuary (188 221 331 707 316 9 248 431 172 638 639). Do not undergo extensive migrations (1465). In the northern Gulf of Mexico, tagging studies indicate that there is little or no exchange of fish between areas east and west of the Mississippi River; as fish age, the tend to converge on the Mississippi River from both the east and west (1463).

Juvenile: Juveniles from the extreme edges of the range tend to "drift" back to the breeding area toward the center of the range (Mississippi delta) probably as a response to currents. Most movement of older fish is inshore/offshore with little east-west movement noted (638 639). Adults and maturing juveniles (80-105 nun SL) migrate from estuaries to open Gulf waters to overwinter or spawn from late summer to winter, with peak movement occurring from October to January (188 331 606 707 172). Some diffuse emigration of larger individuals occurs throughout the year (431). One study reports large schools migrating offshore in June (751). This emigration appears to be size related (1721, but may also be influenced by environmental parameters (431). Adults in the Gulf begin an apparent offshore movement in October from the shallow waters inshore, and begin returning in February. Recent research indicates that the lipid content of the menhaden has an effect on the time of movement; as fish metamorphose from larvae to sub-adults lipid content and energy content increase. Fish with high lipid contents migrate first in response to small changes in temperature and those with lower lipid content migrate later or not at all (751 172).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Menhaden spawn in coastal and offshore waters in the winter. Larvae are found in greatest densities over the inner to middle continental shelf with peak densities occurring in February during one study (639). They spend 3-5 wk in offshore waters before moving into the shallow areas of estuaries and their tributaries where they transform into juveniles. Juveniles move to open and deeper estuarine waters where they remain until the following fall. Adults live in inshore waters during the spring and summer, and offshore during the fall and winter months (117 409 655 172 507).

Substrate: inhabits water column, with no direct use of the substrate apparent. It is assumed soft mud substrates are preferred because of their generally dense benthic populations and richer organic content (120).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs: Collected in the wild from 17-20 C (119). Turner collected eggs and larvae at water temperatures from 10-23 C (737).

Juveniles/adults: Collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures of 20.5-30.0 C (664). Water temperature preference for this species lies above 12.0 and below 30.0, but they have been taken in waters over a range extending from 2.50 to 35.50 C. Temperature tolerances have also been observed to be quite wide at lower salinity levels. Active avoidance of temperatures above 30.0 C has been reported as well as a kill occurring at 39.0 C (470 331 136 751 226 117 561).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body: Euryhaline (891). Gulf menhaden have been collected in water salinities ranging from fresh to hypersaline (331 707 751 226 638 119). Springer and Woodburn (664) collected specimens at 6.6-34.2 ppt in Tampa Bay. Gravid adults, fertilized eggs, and early larvae are typically associated with the higher salinities of the open Gulf of Mexico ranging 29 ppt and higher. Turner (737) collected eggs and larvae at salinities of 25-35 ppt. Post larvae and juveniles occupy a wider range of tolerance from 0 ppt to as high as 60 ppt, but show their most prominent occurrence in waters ca. 10 ppt (327). Non-gravid and developing adults occupy mid-range salinities in the deeper part of estuaries with high abundances at 20-25 ppt reported (751 561). Mass mortalities have been reported due to salinities of 80 ppt or greater.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, separate sexes, oviparous with external fertilization. Multiple (fractional or intermittent) spawners; ova mature and are spawned in bunches over an extended season (1465).

Mating/Spawning: Actual spawning in the wild has not been observed (248 1465). Information is based on capture of eggs, larvae, spent adults, and laboratory fertilizations. Because of the preponderance of females in his samples, Turner(737) concluded that sexual separation occurs during the spawning season. Most spawning probably occurs off the Mississippi and  Atchafalaya River delta from near shore to about 97 km offshore over water depths of 2 to 111 m deep (409 638 639) with most concentrated between 7.3 and 73.2 m (119). Turner (737) did not collect eggs and larvae more than 15 miles from shore, and reported that they were more abundant off southern than off northern Florida with greatest concentrations within Charlotte Harbor. Spawning off south Florida occurs inside the 10-fathom contour, and most occurs within the 5-fathom curve (737). Gulf menhaden are intermittent spawners showing as many as five peaks during a season in different parts of the Gulf. Springer and Woodburn (664) suggested that menhaden spawn during the winter in the Tampa Bay area. Turner (737) reported a January-February spawning peak off southern Florida. A spawning season usually runs from October through March, but can begin as early as August and last as late as April (707 737). Separate peaks can be observed during the season from November to February (470 707 614 409 9 248 431 638 119).

Fecundity: Actual fecundity for menhaden is difficult to determine as they are intermittent, fractional spawners (409). Studies have shown that fecundity increases significantly with age and length (693 409). Mean number of eggs per fish are: 21,960 in age classes I; 68,655 in age class 11; and 122,062 in age class I11 (693).

Lewis and Roithmayr (409) presented the following equations for estimating fecundity:
[eq]
In F = 9.971 + 0.366(A)
In F = =9.872 + 3.878(1n FL)
F = 12,064.3 + 374.9(W) where: A = age in yes; W = wet weight (gm)
[/eq]
Ahrenholz (1465) provided the following equation for the relationship of the number of eggs and length:
[eq]
E = 0.000051604 (L^3.8775)
[/eq]

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs: Planktonic and pelagic. Eggs are spherical with unsculptured chorion, a faintly segmented yolk, and a single oil droplet. Mean total diameter of eggs is 1.30 mm + 0.05. Hatch rate can vary from 1-3 d depending on ambient water temperature. Eggs incubated at 190-200 C in 30 ppt salinity hatched in 40-42 h. Hatching for menhaden occurs for the most part from October to March (300 638 119). Temperature has been shown to effect the rate of yolk utilization, the time between hatching and first feeding, and the ability of larvae to survive food deprivation (565).

Larvae/juvenile: Larvae reared in the laboratory were 2.6-3.0 mm SL immediately after hatching. Growth rate at 200+-20 C averaged 0.30+-0.03 mm/d through 90 d of rearing. Temperature does not determine size at hatching, size at first feeding, and yolk volume at first feeding (565). Larvae incubated at higher temperatures cannot withstand food deprivation well, and they must find food within three days after hatching at 24 C (565). Transformation from the larval to juvenile form began at approximately 19 mm and was completed at approximately 25 mm SL (300). One study of larvae in the wild showed metamorphosis beginning at 20-21 mm SL and being completed at 30-35 mm SL, while another reported metamorphosis taking place at 30-40 mm TL (172 248). By May, most larvae have metamorphosed into juveniles (707). Juveniles may grow as much as 20-30 mrn/mo and become sub-adults at SL's greater than 85 mm.

Adult: Menhaden mature after two seasons of growth and have a maximum life span of five years (507). The bulk of the population is composed of class 1 and 2 fish with few class 3 and even fewer class 4 fish present (119). Maximum reported age is about 4 years (409). Sizes at maturity range from 147-165 mm FL (508). Lassuy (1419) presented the following length-weight relationship derived from data in Nicholson (508) :
[eq]
In W = 1.202 +0.198 (FL), where; W=live wt (gm), and FL = fork length (cm)
[/eq]
Maximum lengths up to 250 mm have been recorded. Slight sexual dimorphism has been reported for menhaden, but it is insufficient to separate sexes (453 737 327).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Larvae are selective carnivores feeding on zooplankters. After metamorphosis, juveniles and adults are omnivorous filter feeders at the first and second trophic level of the food web ingesting phytoplankton, zooplankton, and detritus (172 248 242 791). They are unique in that much of their stored energy is lipid which results in the highest energy content per gram weight found among estuarine species.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
As predators, gulf menhaden ingest large numbers of planktonic larvae of other species, but the effects of this predation have not been quantified. Its role as a forage species is also in need of more research (119).

Gulf menhaden migration patterns coincide with sequentially available, but spatially separate productivity peaks occurring in different areas of an estuarine system (172).

Known to hybridize with B. smithi along both coasts of Florida (737 823 824 829).

Commercial: Gulf menhaden support the largest single commercial fishery (by weight) in the United States (107 638 639). Landings for 1988 were near 1.4 billion pounds valued at $73.3 million. Statewide Florida menhaden landings for 1991 were 7,027,158 lbs valued at $941,639 (902), although most of these are B. tyrannus, and B. smithi landings are probably also included in this sum. Menhaden are harvested from early April to early October as they move into more shallow inshore areas from their wintering grounds on the middle part of the continental shelf (409). Fishing grounds occur in the area extending from Apalachee, Florida to Matagorda Bay, Texas, but are concentrated in Louisiana and Mississippi waters (118 507 1464).

Schools are located by spotter planes who notify large, refrigerated carrier vessels. Two purse seine boats encircle the school with a net. The captured school is then pumped into the hold of the carrier vessel for processing (508 652). Also caught with gill nets and trawls (791). Although not highly esteemed because they are bony and very oily, they are marketed fresh, salted and canned (791). Menhaden are used primarily for the production of meal, oil, and solubles (791). Small quantities are used for bait and canned pet food .

Recreational: Has no sport fish value since it is a filter feeder with unpalatable meat (652).

Indicator: Larvae used by National Marine Fisheries Service to study uptake and effects of heavy metals on the early life stages of fishes (274).

Ecological Role: Extremely important forage fish for a variety of piscivorous birds and fish (119). piscine predators include ~ynoscion nebulosus (220). Important in the translocation of energy between estuarine and offshore ecosystems (172).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Restricted to Gulf of Mexico occurring in estuarine and nearshore marine waters to depths of 111 m from Tampa Bay, Florida to Vera Cruz, Mexico (327 788 791 823 891 983). Principal region of abundance is from Appalachicola, Florida to Galveston, Texas (119 188 327 409 565 585).

Within Study Area: Found only on the west coast of Florida from about Florida Bay north (409 565 585 788 791 891). Dahlberg (823) found B. smithi to be much more common than B. patronus in Florida west coast estuaries. Juveniles commonly occur in all estuaries from Tampa Bay northward, but decrease in numbers to the south (824 1052 1053) .

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Eggs and larvae spend 3-5 wk in offshore waters as currents carry them into estuaries (707 791). Juveniles are nektonic and schooling. Adults are pelagic and schooling, usually found in shallow waters (172 707 751 791). Caught in waters as deep as 60 m (791). Adult migrate offshore for spawning (791 1419).

Larvae are carried from the central breeding grounds for 3-5 weeks by currents and are thought to be distributed along near shore areas throughout the range predominantly by long shore current (639). Larvae migrate into estuaries in late fall and early winter through late May with peak movement into Texas and Louisiana tidal passes occurring between November and early April. They are then carried through open bays and into shallow estuarine areas (tidal creeks and ponds) by tidal flow when ca. 15-25 nun. They may then move past the brackish-freshwater areas and utilize such areas as nursery grounds (655). As larvae metamorphose into juveniles they move into deeper, higher salinity areas of the estuary (188 221 331 707 316 9 248 431 172 638 639). Do not undergo extensive migrations (1465). In the northern Gulf of Mexico, tagging studies indicate that there is little or no exchange of fish between areas east and west of the Mississippi River; as fish age, the tend to converge on the Mississippi River from both the east and west (1463).

Juvenile: Juveniles from the extreme edges of the range tend to "drift" back to the breeding area toward the center of the range (Mississippi delta) probably as a response to currents. Most movement of older fish is inshore/offshore with little east-west movement noted (638 639). Adults and maturing juveniles (80-105 nun SL) migrate from estuaries to open Gulf waters to overwinter or spawn from late summer to winter, with peak movement occurring from October to January (188 331 606 707 172). Some diffuse emigration of larger individuals occurs throughout the year (431). One study reports large schools migrating offshore in June (751). This emigration appears to be size related (1721, but may also be influenced by environmental parameters (431). Adults in the Gulf begin an apparent offshore movement in October from the shallow waters inshore, and begin returning in February. Recent research indicates that the lipid content of the menhaden has an effect on the time of movement; as fish metamorphose from larvae to sub-adults lipid content and energy content increase. Fish with high lipid contents migrate first in response to small changes in temperature and those with lower lipid content migrate later or not at all (751 172).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: Menhaden spawn in coastal and offshore waters in the winter. Larvae are found in greatest densities over the inner to middle continental shelf with peak densities occurring in February during one study (639). They spend 3-5 wk in offshore waters before moving into the shallow areas of estuaries and their tributaries where they transform into juveniles. Juveniles move to open and deeper estuarine waters where they remain until the following fall. Adults live in inshore waters during the spring and summer, and offshore during the fall and winter months (117 409 655 172 507).

Substrate: inhabits water column, with no direct use of the substrate apparent. It is assumed soft mud substrates are preferred because of their generally dense benthic populations and richer organic content (120).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs: Collected in the wild from 17-20 C (119). Turner collected eggs and larvae at water temperatures from 10-23 C (737).

Juveniles/adults: Collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures of 20.5-30.0 C (664). Water temperature preference for this species lies above 12.0 and below 30.0, but they have been taken in waters over a range extending from 2.50 to 35.50 C. Temperature tolerances have also been observed to be quite wide at lower salinity levels. Active avoidance of temperatures above 30.0 C has been reported as well as a kill occurring at 39.0 C (470 331 136 751 226 117 561).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content: Euryhaline (891). Gulf menhaden have been collected in water salinities ranging from fresh to hypersaline (331 707 751 226 638 119). Springer and Woodburn (664) collected specimens at 6.6-34.2 ppt in Tampa Bay. Gravid adults, fertilized eggs, and early larvae are typically associated with the higher salinities of the open Gulf of Mexico ranging 29 ppt and higher. Turner (737) collected eggs and larvae at salinities of 25-35 ppt. Post larvae and juveniles occupy a wider range of tolerance from 0 ppt to as high as 60 ppt, but show their most prominent occurrence in waters ca. 10 ppt (327). Non-gravid and developing adults occupy mid-range salinities in the deeper part of estuaries with high abundances at 20-25 ppt reported (751 561). Mass mortalities have been reported due to salinities of 80 ppt or greater.

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, separate sexes, oviparous with external fertilization. Multiple (fractional or intermittent) spawners; ova mature and are spawned in bunches over an extended season (1465).

Mating/Spawning: Actual spawning in the wild has not been observed (248 1465). Information is based on capture of eggs, larvae, spent adults, and laboratory fertilizations. Because of the preponderance of females in his samples, Turner(737) concluded that sexual separation occurs during the spawning season. Most spawning probably occurs off the Mississippi and  Atchafalaya River delta from near shore to about 97 km offshore over water depths of 2 to 111 m deep (409 638 639) with most concentrated between 7.3 and 73.2 m (119). Turner (737) did not collect eggs and larvae more than 15 miles from shore, and reported that they were more abundant off southern than off northern Florida with greatest concentrations within Charlotte Harbor. Spawning off south Florida occurs inside the 10-fathom contour, and most occurs within the 5-fathom curve (737). Gulf menhaden are intermittent spawners showing as many as five peaks during a season in different parts of the Gulf. Springer and Woodburn (664) suggested that menhaden spawn during the winter in the Tampa Bay area. Turner (737) reported a January-February spawning peak off southern Florida. A spawning season usually runs from October through March, but can begin as early as August and last as late as April (707 737). Separate peaks can be observed during the season from November to February (470 707 614 409 9 248 431 638 119).

Fecundity: Actual fecundity for menhaden is difficult to determine as they are intermittent, fractional spawners (409). Studies have shown that fecundity increases significantly with age and length (693 409). Mean number of eggs per fish are: 21,960 in age classes I; 68,655 in age class 11; and 122,062 in age class I11 (693).

Lewis and Roithmayr (409) presented the following equations for estimating fecundity:

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Eggs: Planktonic and pelagic. Eggs are spherical with unsculptured chorion, a faintly segmented yolk, and a single oil droplet. Mean total diameter of eggs is 1.30 mm + 0.05. Hatch rate can vary from 1-3 d depending on ambient water temperature. Eggs incubated at 190-200 C in 30 ppt salinity hatched in 40-42 h. Hatching for menhaden occurs for the most part from October to March (300 638 119). Temperature has been shown to effect the rate of yolk utilization, the time between hatching and first feeding, and the ability of larvae to survive food deprivation (565).

Larvae/juvenile: Larvae reared in the laboratory were 2.6-3.0 mm SL immediately after hatching. Growth rate at 200+-20 C averaged 0.30+-0.03 mm/d through 90 d of rearing. Temperature does not determine size at hatching, size at first feeding, and yolk volume at first feeding (565). Larvae incubated at higher temperatures cannot withstand food deprivation well, and they must find food within three days after hatching at 24 C (565). Transformation from the larval to juvenile form began at approximately 19 mm and was completed at approximately 25 mm SL (300). One study of larvae in the wild showed metamorphosis beginning at 20-21 mm SL and being completed at 30-35 mm SL, while another reported metamorphosis taking place at 30-40 mm TL (172 248). By May, most larvae have metamorphosed into juveniles (707). Juveniles may grow as much as 20-30 mrn/mo and become sub-adults at SL's greater than 85 mm.

Adult: Menhaden mature after two seasons of growth and have a maximum life span of five years (507). The bulk of the population is composed of class 1 and 2 fish with few class 3 and even fewer class 4 fish present (119). Maximum reported age is about 4 years (409). Sizes at maturity range from 147-165 mm FL (508). Lassuy (1419) presented the following length-weight relationship derived from data in Nicholson (508) :
[eq]
In W = 1.202 +0.198 (FL), where; W=live wt (gm), and FL = fork length (cm)
[/eq]
Maximum lengths up to 250 mm have been recorded. Slight sexual dimorphism has been reported for menhaden, but it is insufficient to separate sexes (453 737 327).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Larvae are selective carnivores feeding on zooplankters. After metamorphosis, juveniles and adults are omnivorous filter feeders at the first and second trophic level of the food web ingesting phytoplankton, zooplankton, and detritus (172 248 242 791). They are unique in that much of their stored energy is lipid which results in the highest energy content per gram weight found among estuarine species.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
As predators, gulf menhaden ingest large numbers of planktonic larvae of other species, but the effects of this predation have not been quantified. Its role as a forage species is also in need of more research (119).

Gulf menhaden migration patterns coincide with sequentially available, but spatially separate productivity peaks occurring in different areas of an estuarine system (172).

Known to hybridize with B. smithi along both coasts of Florida (737 823 824 829).
